paragraphs: “We found him in his study, lying on his back on the floor, his head smashed in,” said the prosecutor.
“That’s horrible!” Mitya shuddered. He put his elbows on the table and hid his face in his right hand.
“Let us go on,” Nikolay Parfenovitch put in. “So what drove you to this hatred? I believe you have stated in public that it came from jealousy?”
“Well, yes, jealousy. And not only jealousy.”
“A quarrel over money?”
“Yes, over money, too.”
“There was a dispute over three thousand roubles, I believe, which you claimed as part of your inheritance?”

“Three thousand! More, more,” cried Mitya hotly. “More than six thousand, more than ten, maybe. I told everyone, I shouted it at them. But I made up my mind to settle for three thousand. I needed that three thousand desperately ... so that packet of notes for three thousand, which I knew he kept under his pillow, ready for Grushenka, I counted as simply stolen from me. Yes, gentlemen, I regarded it as mine, as my own property....”
The prosecutor gave the investigating lawyer a meaningful look and managed to wink at him on the sly.
“We will return to that later,” the lawyer said quickly. “You will let us make a note of that point and write it down: that you regarded that money as your own property?”

“Write it down, by all means. I know that’s one more fact against me, but I’m not afraid of facts, and I bring them up against myself. Do you hear? Do you know, gentlemen, you take me for a different sort of man from what I am,” he added, suddenly gloomy and downcast. “You have before you a man of honor, a man of the highest honor. Above all—don’t lose sight of this—a man who has done a lot of nasty things, but who has always been, and still is, honorable at bottom, deep inside. I don’t know how to put it. That’s exactly what’s made me miserable all my life: I longed to be honorable, I was, so to speak, a martyr to the sense of honor, hunting for it with a lantern, the lantern of Diogenes. And yet all my life I’ve done filthy things like all of us, gentlemen ... that is, like me alone. That was a mistake, like me alone, me alone!... Gentlemen, my head aches ...” His brows drew together with pain. “You see, gentlemen, I couldn’t stand the sight of him. There was something ignoble in him, something shameless, that trampled on everything sacred, something sneering and irreverent, loathsome, loathsome. But now that he’s dead, I feel differently.”
“What do you mean?”
“I don’t feel differently, but I wish I hadn’t hated him so.”
“Do you feel remorse?”
“No, not remorse, don’t write that. I’m no great prize myself, I’m not very beautiful, so I had no right to find him repulsive. That’s what I mean. Write that down, if you like.”
Saying this, Mitya became deeply mournful. He had grown gloomier and gloomier as the inquiry went on.

Just then another unexpected scene took place. Grushenka had been removed, but not taken far. She was only in the second room along from the blue room where the examination was being held. It was a small room with one window, just past the large room where they had danced and feasted so lavishly. She sat there with nobody beside her but Maximov, who was terribly dejected and terribly frightened and clung to her side as if for protection. One of the peasants, with a metal plate on his chest, stood at their door. Grushenka was crying. All at once her grief was more than she could bear. She leapt up, flung out her arms and, with a loud wail, ran out of the room to him, to her Mitya. It was so sudden that nobody had time to stop her. Mitya heard her cry, trembled, jumped up and, with a yell, dashed to meet her, not knowing what he was doing. But they were not allowed to come together, though they could see each other. Men seized him by the arms. He struggled and tried to break free. It took three or four of them to hold him. She was seized too, and he saw her reaching out her arms to him and crying aloud as they carried her off. When the scene was over, he came to himself again, sitting in the same place as before, across from the investigating lawyer, and calling out to them:
“What do you want with her? Why do you torment her? She’s done nothing, nothing!...”
The lawyers tried to calm him. About ten minutes passed like this. Finally Mihail Makarovitch, who had been out of the room, came in hurriedly and said to the prosecutor in a loud, agitated voice:
“She’s been taken away, she’s downstairs. Will you let me say one word to this unhappy man, gentlemen? In your presence, gentlemen, in your presence.”
“By all means, Mihail Makarovitch,” the investigating lawyer replied. “In this case we have no objection.”

“Listen, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, my dear fellow,” the police captain began, and on his flushed face was a look of warm, almost fatherly feeling for the unlucky prisoner. “I took your Agrafena Alexandrovna downstairs myself and handed her over to the landlord’s daughters. That old fellow Maximov is with her the whole time. And I comforted her, do you hear? I comforted her and calmed her down. I explained to her that you have to clear yourself, so she mustn’t hinder you or depress you, or you might lose your head and give the wrong evidence. In a word, I talked to her and she understood. She’s a sensible girl, my boy, a good-hearted girl. She wanted to kiss my old hands and beg me to help you. She sent me herself to tell you not to worry about her. And I have to go, my dear fellow, I have to go and tell her you’re calm and easy in your mind about her. So you must be calm, do you understand? I was unfair to her. She is a Christian soul, gentlemen, yes, I tell you, a gentle soul, and not to blame for anything. So what am I to tell her, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Will you sit quietly or not?”

The kindly police captain said a great deal that was out of order. But Grushenka’s suffering, the suffering of a fellow human being, had touched his good heart, and there were tears in his eyes. Mitya jumped up and rushed toward him.

“Forgive me, gentlemen, oh, allow me, allow me!” he cried. “You have the heart of an angel, an angel, Mihail Makarovitch. I thank you for her. I will, I will be calm, cheerful even. Tell her, out of the kindness of your heart, that I am cheerful, perfectly cheerful, that I’ll be laughing in a minute, knowing she has a guardian angel like you. I’ll have finished with all this very soon, and the moment I’m free I’ll be with her, she’ll see, let her wait. Gentlemen,” he said, turning to the two lawyers, “now I’ll open my whole soul to you. I’ll pour it all out. We’ll wrap this up quickly, wrap it up cheerfully. We’ll laugh about it in the end, won’t we? But, gentlemen, that woman is the queen of my heart. Oh, let me tell you that. That one thing I’ll tell you now.... I see I’m among honorable men. She is my light, she is my holy one, and if only you knew! Did you hear her cry, ‘I’ll go to my death with you’? And what have I done for her, a penniless beggar? Why does she love me so? How can a clumsy, ugly brute like me, with my ugly face, deserve a love like that, so that she’s ready to go into exile with me? And how she fell at your feet for my sake, just now!... and yet she’s proud and has done nothing! How can I help adoring her, how can I help crying out and rushing to her as I did just now? Gentlemen, forgive me! But now, now I’m comforted.”

And he sank back in his chair, hid his face in his hands and burst into tears. But they were happy tears. He pulled himself together at once. The old police captain looked very pleased, and so did the lawyers. They sensed that the examination was entering a new phase. When the police captain went out, Mitya was positively gay.

“Now, gentlemen, I’m at your disposal, entirely at your disposal. And if it weren’t for all these petty details, we’d understand each other in a minute. There I go again with the details. I’m at your disposal, gentlemen, but I tell you we must trust each other, you me and I you, or there’ll be no end to it. I’m saying this for your sake. To business, gentlemen, to business, and don’t rummage in my soul. Don’t pester me with trifles, but ask me only about facts and what matters, and I’ll satisfy you at once. And damn the details!”
So spoke Mitya. The interrogation began again.
